data.title: Pezinok – Starý zámok II, a timber fortlet in the Lesser Carpathians
data.excerpt: On a long narrow ridge of the Lesser Carpathians above Pezinok stood a timber fortlet some 200 m long that watched over the less well known routes between the Trnava Hills and Záhorie. Excavation revealed a multi-storey log tower on a rocky crag, a glass vessel of Italian origin and numerous iron arrowheads from the armed assault that ended the site at the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries.
data.metaTitle: Pezinok – Starý zámok II: a timber fortlet
data.metaDescription: A narrow fortlet 200 m long with a timber tower on a ridge of the Lesser Carpathians above Pezinok, built in the 13th century and destroyed by attack and fire.

children.text: The medieval fortlet of Pezinok – Zámok II lies on a long narrow ridge of the Lesser Carpathians, above the confluence of the mountain streams Sedláčkov jarok and Blatina in the Cajlanská (Hrubá) valley, not far from the former woodcutters' hamlet of Rybníček. Besides the main valley, the fortlet thus also controlled several side valleys that allowed passage from Pezinok towards Záhorie across the Baba saddle or the saddle below Javorina. Its task may have been to protect one of the less well known trade and military routes linking the Carpathian Basin, by way of the Trnava Hills, with the parts of Europe lying further west, above all with Austria and the Kingdom of Bohemia.

Its ground plan was adapted to the cramped mountain terrain – a narrow and long rocky ridge. That is probably also why the fortlet eventually reached a length of as much as about 200 m. The small fort, which on present knowledge cannot be unambiguously identified with any fortified position of the High Middle Ages known from the written sources, lay away from the main lines of the trade and military routes linking the Kingdom of Hungary with the areas of Europe lying further west; it evidently did, however, control one or two crossings of primarily regional importance that connected the Trnava Hills and Záhorie. One of the approach routes to the fortified area ran from the north along the crest of the ridge and entered the fortlet through a neck ditch cut into the rock massif, as yet not examined in detail. Another approach route led from the north to the small saddle between Srnčí vŕšok and the rocky tooth with the timber buildings on its summit, along a track climbing up the western hillside, today largely destroyed by the now abandoned quarry.

Unlike the route along the ridge, it is attested in the terrain by a still distinct cutting and by finds of material culture of the High Middle Ages. According to the archaeological finds, this relatively comfortable approach route, which could nevertheless be well controlled directly from the fortification, ended precisely in the small saddle, and perhaps some of the everyday activities connected with the function and the economic running of the fortification took place here. Traces of the originally assumed farm shelters have not, however, been attested here so far. From the small saddle a steep path climbed from the south towards the fortlet, and it had to cross a ditch about 4.2 m wide cut into the rock, still distinct today, perhaps along a narrow belt of rock not even 1 m wide and therefore easy to defend, between the ditch and the eastern drop of the crag. The traces in the terrain are not, however, sufficient to reconstruct how the entrance into the small fort itself was arranged. A shallow groove cut into the rock bedrock in front of the ditch does not rule out the possibility that on the outer side it was supplemented by a light field obstacle resembling a fence.

According to the archaeological finds, the summit of the rocky tooth was occupied by a multi-storey timber building of tower-like character, most probably of log construction, which, judging by the fragments of daub, was originally protected at least in part by a layer of clay plaster for fire-proofing, insulating and aesthetic reasons. The dimensions of the “tower” are not unambiguous; they had to be adapted to the limited dimensions of the crag and to the laws of statics, but the length of the walls evidently exceeded 5 m. One of its corners was underpinned by a block of imported sandstone, which was continued by “stone footings” of dry-laid quarry stone and by traces of burnt beams. Approximately in the middle of the feature was a cutting into the rock bedrock about 1 m deep, measuring 2.9 × 1.7–2.3 m. The pit probably served as the underground space of the timber tower-like buildings of the “rock castles”, which ensured the anchoring and stability of the higher structures, but it could also have been used to store supplies. Directly adjoining the “tower” was another timber building, with its longer axis parallel to the axis of the ridge (3.6 × 1.5 m). Its western part was sunk into the rock bedrock. The floor, and probably also the lining of the rock walls, consisted, judging by the remains of charcoal, perhaps of planks. Its eastern part is missing; the terrain here falls away steeply into the valley that leads to the Rybníček forester's lodge. One possibility is that the slope collapsed here together with the remains of the building. Another variant does not rule out the possibility that its side projected out over the drop in the manner of a balcony supported by timber. Unlike the nearby tower, building No. 2 was evidently only a single-roomed structure with a single storey. Relatively little is still known about the interior furnishing of the buildings of small fortified positions of the High Middle Ages. On the basis of the finds and of analogies, however, it is possible to assume that they were basically furnished with wooden furniture (a table, a bed and, judging by the keys to locking mechanisms, probably also chests and caskets). Short iron hinges may come either from furniture or from shutters or flaps of the window openings. Besides the wooden products, which have not survived, pottery belonged to the equipment, and a fragment of a glass vessel evidently points to at least occasional stays by a higher social stratum at the fortlet. An interesting feature, by comparison with other similar fortified positions, is the relatively small proportion of craft tools needed for the construction, maintenance and operation of the fort in the find material. Agricultural implements are entirely absent, which may also reflect the specific function of the fortlet, which had no direct economic hinterland. Archaeological excavation has so far produced no unambiguous insights into the manner in which Starý zámok II was fortified. Apart from the timber tower with the ditch in front of it in its southern, dominant part, the defence evidently relied above all on the steep, barely passable slopes.

So far it has not been possible to detect evidence of a masonry or a timber-and-earth defensive wall. Behind building No. 2 the extraction area of the former quarry already began, and the whole central, perhaps most important part of the medieval small fort fell irretrievably victim to it. Judging by the pointed cuts in the hitherto preserved rock face of the original crag, it cannot be ruled out that one or two pointed ditches separated both buildings from the original ridge. These could have closed off the approach route along the ridge to the core, or to the oldest part of “Starý zámok”. Apart from the fire, the violent demise of Starý zámok II is indicated by numerous iron arrowheads, according to which the enemy advanced along the cart track towards Srnčí vŕšok and then to the fortification itself. It can be assumed that incendiary substances were attached to some of the arrows, intended to undermine the determination of the defenders or at least to keep them partly occupied with extinguishing the fire that had been started. The chronological definition of the relatively short existence of the oldest phase of the development of Starý zámok II near Pezinok, and of its demise, is made possible above all by the accompanying archaeological material. Among the pottery forms, pots with a chalice-like everted mouth predominated, but there were also jugs with broad handles divided by grooves. The finds make it possible to place the destruction horizon of the timber fortlet in the second half of the 13th to the beginning of the 14th century, while the silver Viennese pfennigs struck by Přemysl Otakar II can, with a certain caution, narrow this period down to the 1270s. Its origin can thus be assumed in the second half of the 13th century. Some of the arrowheads have, on present knowledge, an unusual, partly archaic form for 13th-century combat projectiles. Some of them originally belonged to specialised hunting points, which in this form survived in eastern Europe deep into the High Middle Ages. If all the arrows are connected with the taking of Starý zámok, then they may point to several interesting facts. For example to the ethnicity of some of the defenders of the small fort. In the second half of the 13th and at the beginning of the 14th century the Hungarian rulers were fond of settling border guards of east European steppe origin in the frontier regions, for example Polovtsians and Cumans, among whom such arrowheads had a long tradition. Nor can it be ruled out, however, that at a time when the defenders were running out of arrows suitable for fighting an at least partly armoured opponent, they resorted in their need to munitions otherwise intended for hunting game.

On present knowledge, no other buildings arose on the summit of the crag, where the log tower originally stood, after its demise. So far it is above all the surface finds from the rubble beneath the rear wall of the quarry on the eastern slope of the ridge and from the surroundings of the massive neck ditch in the natural break of slope to the north of the extraction pit, slowly becoming overgrown with forest, that attest that the position did not fall into oblivion later either and was at least occasionally used as a strongpoint or signalling point until the turn of the 15th and 16th centuries at the latest. For operational and perhaps also defensive reasons the fortification was then gradually extended northwards, towards the pronounced neck ditch. Archaeological excavation gave no unambiguous answer to the question of whether Starý zámok II can be identified with that castle in Pezinok which, according to the Klosterneuburg Chronicle, the Bohemian king Přemysl Otakar II occupied in the spring of 1271, yet we cannot rule out this possibility. The archaeological finds allow only a broad dating of the armed action in which its oldest part came to an end, and this despite the finds of coins struck by this ruler in the territory of Austria. Compared with Starý zámok I, more indications speak in favour of this possibility: – the timber small fort stood at the time of the Bohemian king's expansion into western Slovakia; – a rocky crag heightened by a log building of at least two storeys could have given the impression of a strong and defensible tower; – at some point in that period a fight took place here that had fatal consequences for the fortification. One must not, however, forget the other military actions in which the castle at Pezinok and the whole west of present-day Slovakia played an active role at the close of the 13th and the beginning of the 14th century; – despite the fact that the fortlet cannot have had a large garrison, on the basis of some of the finds the presence of a social elite from the ranks of the nobility can be reckoned with here (for example the glass vessel of Italian origin, certainly valuable at that time). At present, however, on the basis of new finds uncovered during the reconstruction of Pezinok Castle standing in the town itself, which attest the existence of a stone castle here already in the course of the 13th century, it seems that it was this castle that entered the annals and is the castle that the chronicler thought worth mentioning when describing the military successes of the Bohemian king – and not a less important, and moreover timber, small fort lost deep in the mountains.

Starý zámok II near Pezinok belongs to a group of as yet relatively little known timber or timber-and-earth fortlets of the 13th to the beginning of the 14th century, some of which lie at a relatively short distance from the substantially better known stone castles (for example Pajštún – Dračí hrádok, Pezinok – Starý zámok I and II, Smolenice – Kalvária, Dobrá Voda – Pod Mariášom, perhaps Červený Kameň and so on). Before more extensive archaeological excavations of these pairs we can only speculate about their chronological succession, or possibly about a shorter period of overlap between them. It could thus be a matter of the gradual replacement of older, slowly obsolescent fortifications by more modern ones, which were, however, more demanding both in construction and financially. Besides these, timber-and-earth fortlets also appear at strategic places on the edge of or inside the valleys of the Lesser Carpathians (as if in accordance with the principle of keeping watch but not being too conspicuous – Železník, Pod Mariášom, Dračí hrádok, Starý zámok II). Judging by the accompanying material, most of them were established in the course of the 13th century, perhaps after the Mongol invasion, and came to an end at the close of the 13th or at the beginning of the 14th century, in the period of the fighting between the Kingdom of Hungary and the Kingdom of Bohemia, or possibly in the subsequent troubled times connected with the reign of the last Árpáds and the onset of feudal anarchy. Only in the case of the Kuchyňa castle and Starý zámok II does the archaeological material make it possible to assume a longer development, ending sometime in the second half of the 15th or at the very beginning of the 16th century. In the case of Kuchyňa, and perhaps also of Starý zámok, the older fortification was gradually supplemented by stone architecture, the remains of which have also survived at Dračí hrádok. Timber-and-earth fortifications in the form of small forts appeared again, however, in the 15th century (for example Ostriež near Brezová pod Bradlom), when some of the older prehistoric to early medieval hillforts were also partly revitalised.

The text is taken, with only minor adjustments, from the conclusion of an article by Zdenko Farkaš: STREDOVEKÉ OPEVNENIE STARÝ ZÁMOK II PRI PEZINKU (The medieval fortification Starý zámok II near Pezinok), ZBORNÍK SLOVENSKÉHO NÁRODNÉHO MÚZEA CIX 2015 ARCHEOLÓGIA 25, which you can read in full at
